Credit : Research Gate) Review essay By Tegegne Tefera Most Ethiopians have direct experience of an Iddir. When a death occurs in a neighbourhood, the association to which the households belong takes on the practical work — the tent, the chairs, the cooking, the arrangements for the burial — and pays the bereaved family a fixed sum set by its own rules. It is funded by members’ monthly contributions. No government office approves it, no donor pays for it, and nobody running it was appointed from outside. This essay is about why that familiar arrangement may bear on a question Professor Messay Kebede raises in his book Ethiopian Modernization: Opportunities and Derailments , and about a working paper that takes up his argument at the point where he leaves it. The question the book asks For more than a century Ethiopia has tried to modernise. The emperors built schools, ministries and a modern army. The Derg promised socialism and an end to feudal privilege. The EPRDF promised ethnic self-rule and a developmental state. These projects differed widely in ideology, but the outcome in each case shared certain features: power concentrated at the centre, little room for organised society, and recurring conflict over control of the state. Messay’s book, which is freely available online through the University of Dayton, asks why the outcome has been so similar under such different governments. It moves from theories of modernization and Ethiopia’s long history of survival through the imperial era, the student movement, the Derg and the ethnonationalist period, and ends with a roadmap for change. Readers need not accept every historical judgment in it to find it useful. It offers Ethiopians of different backgrounds and generations a common starting point for a discussion that often divides into arguments about one ruler, one period or one community. Derailment Messay’s central idea is derailment. Ethiopia did not fail to acquire modern things. It acquired a great many of them: schools, bureaucracies, weapons, political doctrines and new forms of organisation. The difficulty lay in what they were used for. Modern means were repeatedly put to an older purpose, which was keeping power concentrated in the hands of whoever held the centre. This is why a change of ideology produced so little change in the result. The Ethiopian state, Messay writes, is designed to “suck all power from the society” in favour of a group and, in the end, of one person. He is equally direct about the remedy. Neither conflict nor derailment will end without reform that “gives back some power of the state to the society,” so that communities and individuals move from “passive subjects into active participants.” He adds a warning. New institutions remain “empty shells” unless people develop the habits and values that make them work. A constitution cannot by itself teach anyone to hold leaders to account. What the book leaves open Two questions follow from that remedy, and the book does not set out to answer either. The first is what power would be given back to. Society is not a single body that can receive it. Power needs somewhere to live: organisations that ordinary people belong to, run themselves, and are able to defend. The second is who would hand it over. If the state is built to draw power upward, asking those who hold it to give some of it away is asking a good deal. Reform of this kind is more likely to happen, and more likely to last, where an organised society already exists to ask for it and to hold it in place. Messay sets out the direction of change clearly. He does not set out the institutions through which ordinary Ethiopians would receive, exercise and defend returned power. That is not a defect. His question is why modernization derailed, and he answers it at length. But it leaves an opening, and the working paper Modernization from Below takes up his argument at that point. It extends his account rather than disputing it. Its candidate for the missing institution is the Iddir. Why the Iddir? Not because it is traditional or familiar. The case rests on properties that follow from Messay’s own diagnosis: It pays its own way. Most Iddirs are funded entirely by members’ monthly contributions rather than by the state or by donors. Their treasuries are not government grants, and their officers do not hold their positions through a party. The people who pay in are the people who decide. This is the point that separates the Iddir from most comparable institutions, and it is easy to pass over. Churches are funded by the faithful, and many cooperatives by member shares; being paid for by its members is not in itself unusual. What is unusual is that the rules governing the fund are written by the members in assembly and amended there, that the officers who hold it are elected by the contributors and replaced by them, and that no body above the association can direct what it does with what it has. Funds contributed by members but governed by someone else leave those members as beneficiaries. Funds governed by the members who contribute them make those members participants, which is the change Messay’s remedy calls for. It is open across divisions. It is organised around death, which everyone faces. Membership is therefore not limited in principle by ethnicity, religion or class, and as Iddirs spread through the twentieth century many came to include mixed communities. It runs by rules. Iddirs have written by-laws, elected or rotating officers, accounts and penalties. Membership is chosen rather than inherited. It outlives its leaders. Officers are replaced and the institution continues. In some Iddirs every household takes its turn in office. It is Ethiopian, and it is modern. The Iddir developed among migrants to Addis Ababa in the early twentieth century and spread across the country. It is not a survival from the past. It is an instance of what Messay calls the “Ethiopianization” of modernity, produced from below during the same century in which the state-led version derailed. None of this means that every Iddir is a model. Some exclude outsiders, and some penalise members who cannot pay. The claim concerns what the institution is capable of, and how widely that capability already exists. The objection that Iddirs are too small This is the first objection most readers will raise. A single Iddir has a small treasury, serves one neighbourhood, and buries the dead. How could it matter to the fate of a country? The objection measures the wrong quantity. It looks at the size of one Iddir rather than at how many there are and how many people they reach. One estimate puts the number of Iddirs in Addis Ababa alone at more than 7,800, covering over 85 percent of households. Few institutions in Ethiopia, public or private, reach that many people, and almost none do so without being paid for by the state. Iddirs have also worked at scale before. Between 2004 and 2009, some 270 Iddirs took part in community care for people living with HIV, alongside government, health agencies and NGOs. Commercial banks now offer accounts designed for Iddirs, and Iddirs were among the founding shareholders of Addis International Bank. The commercial sector has evidently found them substantial enough to design products for. They have also operated under the imperial government, under the Derg and under the EPRDF, and they continue to operate now. Few Ethiopian institutions have that record. Their smallness was partly a choice. Researchers have found that Iddirs often avoided wider roles, and that many declined to register, because they were wary of state interference. Where coordination between Iddirs did occur, it tended to arrive from above: a confederation of 395 Iddirs was proposed in Addis Ababa in 1972, at a time when the imperial government appears to have treated Iddirs as a means of preserving the existing order. Remaining local was, in part, a way of remaining independent. That points to the more substantial answer. The usual way for an organisation to become large is to merge into a single body with a head office. But a head office is also the easiest thing for a government to take over, since replacing the people who run it gives control of everything beneath it. Modernization from Below proposes a different route, and is careful about the word for it. It does not propose a federation, because a federation is a body set above its members, and that body is what tends to be captured — the confederation proposed in 1972 would have had one, and the British friendly societies had one, whose central administration the state first used and then dispensed with. What it proposes is a network. Thousands of independent Iddirs would keep their own rules, members and funds while cooperating on agreed tasks, such as confirming that a member who has moved to another city is in good standing with their own Iddir. Nothing would sit above them. This is less unfamiliar than it sounds. In parts of Kembata, Iddirs already cooperate within a wider community institution, the Hera, without giving up their own affairs. What has changed is the technology. Coordination used to require a central office because the shared records had to be kept somewhere, and whoever kept them acquired a position of authority that the arrangement itself did not require. Records can now be held in common without being held in one place. This does not create trust, which Iddirs already have. It allows institutions that work locally to cooperate at a distance without building a new centre that someone could take over. On this view the number of Iddirs matters more than the size of any one of them. Taking control of thousands of small, self-funded associations would have to be done separately in each case, and in each case in front of that association’s own members. An independent economic base This leads to the point that may matter most if Messay’s conclusions are to be acted on. His diagnosis is economic as much as political. Under the old order and under all three modern governments, he writes, “everything (social status, wealth, opportunities, etc.), revolves around one’s closeness to the exercise of power.” Holding the state means controlling access to jobs, land, licences, credit and standing. This is why competition for the state becomes competition for access to everything else. If that is right, giving power back to society cannot mean political rights alone. A citizen may vote and an association may be legally registered, but where livelihoods depend on the goodwill of officials, participation remains fragile. Power returned to a society with no resources of its own can be withdrawn again. Messay’s epigraph puts the matter directly: “People have only those rights that they can effectively defend.” Defending rights requires organisation, and organisation requires resources that someone else cannot simply withdraw. This is where the Iddir is unusual. Its money comes from its members rather than from closeness to power, and, as above, the members govern it themselves. In Messay’s own terms it is a small but real instance of resources that are not allocated by proximity to the state. The effects extend beyond the Iddir. A family supported at a funeral has less need of a patron. A neighbourhood with an organised, self-funded association can negotiate with local officials rather than petition them; a study of Iddirs in Addis Ababa found that associations funding neighbourhood projects from their own members’ contributions appeared to negotiate from a stronger position. Each contribution is modest. But it is paid by most households in the capital, every month, year after year, under rules the members write and through officers they replace. Taken together that is a large and continuous flow of resources governed by citizens outside the state’s system of allocation, and little else in Ethiopia can be described that way. One qualification is needed here, because the figure invites a misreading. Nobody commands that flow. There is no body above the Iddirs that could spend it, and the working paper argues that the absence of such a body is the point of the arrangement rather than a gap in it. The figure does not describe a fund available to anyone. It describes a population that has somewhere to turn other than a patron, and a household that does not need a patron at the moment of bereavement is to that extent less dependent on one. What this could develop into once Iddirs cooperate — through shared protection against shocks, and through other forms of community economic organisation built alongside them — is a question that deserves study rather than a promise. A caution belongs here as well. Because the Iddir’s funds and membership have value to others, attempts have been made to use them. Under the Derg, Iddirs were enlisted to promote state objectives. In Akaki, officials used Iddir leaders to collect contributions for state projects, and poorer members who could not pay were excluded from their own Iddir’s benefits. Elsewhere officials sought to redirect member funds, or to use Iddir meetings for election campaigns. An independent economic base can be captured. The lessons the working paper draws are practical: keep funds to the purpose members agreed, make every movement of money visible to members, place nothing at a centre that anyone could seize, and establish new economic ventures as separate bodies rather than attaching them to the Iddir. The aim is not an Iddir that does everything, but an Iddir that remains independent, around which other independent institutions can grow. The working paper sets out these safeguards, and the record of capture behind them, in detail. Where to read further Messay’s book should be read first on its own terms. It is a serious account of why a century of modernization kept arriving at the same impasse, and it deserves readers well beyond those who already agree with its conclusions. Modernization from Below: Iddir and the Missing Institutional Mediation in Messay Kebede’s Ethiopian Modernization takes his argument a step further, and contains the analysis, evidence and sources behind this essay. It asks where returned power would live, why the Iddir is the strongest candidate, how Iddirs might cooperate at national scale without a head office, and how they might resist capture. It is a working paper offered for correction. It touches on law, anthropology, economics and public administration, and it needs readers in each of those fields, and members of Iddirs, to test it. Readers who want to go further again will find the question of how such a network would actually be built — the rules, the safeguards, the technical arrangements and their costs — worked out in a separate set of papers published under the name Hibreteiddir, Iddirs in union . Those papers are a design proposal rather than a finding. Their design includes elements the working paper does not require, among them treasuries that act only by rule, one for each Iddir and one shared across the network, and a token, Dir. Each Dir is minted on a member’s contribution and owed by the Iddir’s main service Iddir, the association within it that collected the money, which keeps the money and repays the debt by paying members’ claims from it and by buying Dir, so that the Dir in existence equals the debts outstanding. Dir’s legal position is one of the questions those papers leave open. They are offered on the same terms as the working paper and this essay: freely, without attribution, and for correction. The claim in all of this is not that the Iddir resolves Ethiopia’s political difficulties. It is narrower. An institution of the kind Messay’s remedy requires may already exist in Ethiopia, in a form communities have maintained for a hundred years through every change of government, and it is worth examining on those terms. It is not an offer of any token, membership or service, and it is not legal, financial or tax advice. Authors note :Prepared with AI assistance. Works discussed : Messay Kebede. ethiopia.summary: In his review of Professor Messay Kebede's book, "Ethiopian Modernization: Opportunities and Derailments," Tegegne Tefera explores the concept of Iddir, a traditional Ethiopian community association that plays a crucial role in local society. Iddirs manage funeral arrangements and provide financial support to bereaved families through member contributions, operating independently of government oversight. Kebede argues that Ethiopia's modernization efforts have repeatedly failed due to centralized power that stifles organized society and perpetuates conflict. He advocates for reform that redistributes power back to communities, transforming citizens from passive subjects into active participants. Tefera suggests that Iddirs could serve as a model for this change, as they are self-funded, democratically governed, and inclusive across ethnic and social lines. With over 7,800 Iddirs in Addis Ababa alone, their widespread presence and adaptability highlight their potential to foster a more participatory society, challenging the traditional state-centric power dynamics in Ethiopia.

ethiopia.title: Leaked Intelligence: Eritrean-Sudanese Coordination of Drone Attacks on Ethiopia's Mekelle & Assosa - horn review
ethiopia.content: Leaked Intelligence: Eritrean-Sudanese Coordination of Drone Attacks on Ethiopia’s Mekelle & Assosa – HORN REVIEW Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us Search Home Research and Analysis Ethiopia and the World Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Publications Horn Review Journal Articles Policy Briefs The Greater Horn: Monthly Strategic Brief Horn Review Magazine Weekly Geopolitical Report Research Paper Commentary Event Flagship Events Conferences Brainstorming Sessions Team About Us Contact Us 2026-11-24 Leaked Intelligence: Eritrean-Sudanese Coordination of Drone Attacks on Ethiopia’s Mekelle & Assosa 0 Comments Leaked intelligence pointing to alleged coordination between the Eritrean regime and Sudan’s military leadership under General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan to conduct drone attacks against Ethiopian cities of Mekelle and Asosa raises serious concerns about an increasingly coordinated war campaign against the Ethiopian state. According to the reported intelligence, the two sides have discussed preparations for aerial attacks against the cities, allegedly relying on Ethiopian armed opposition groups sheltered within their respective territories to facilitate ground operations. The reported targeting of civilian populations and civilian infrastructure would mark a particularly dangerous escalation, taking the confrontation beyond the familiar dynamics of proxy warfare and into the direct targeting of Ethiopian population centres. The allegations cannot be viewed in isolation from the trajectory of the Eritrean regime’s relations with the Ethiopian state over the past four years. The Isaias Afwerki regime has sustained an increasingly aggressive political and diplomatic campaign built around claims that Ethiopia’s pursuit of secure and diversified access to the Red Sea constitutes a threat to Eritrean sovereignty and territorial integrity. Asmara has consistently portrayed Ethiopia’s legitimate maritime aspirations as an existential security challenge. Yet this rhetoric sits uneasily alongside Eritrea’s own record of hostility towards Ethiopia, including its longstanding hosting, support and facilitation of Ethiopian armed opposition movements seeking to undermine the Ethiopian state. This relationship with anti-Ethiopian armed groups predates the current tensions and has been a feature of Eritrea’s regional posture for much of its post-secession history. More recently, incursions by Eritrean forces extending more than 60 kilometres into Ethiopian territory in late September 2026 have added another dimension to an already deteriorating relationship. The contradiction is difficult to ignore: a government that invokes sovereignty and territorial integrity to portray itself as a victim of Ethiopian ambitions is simultaneously supporting armed movements, invading Ethiopian territory and coordinating airstrikes against Ethiopian cities, seeking to destabilize not only Ethiopia but the wider Horn of Africa and the Red Sea corridor. Hence, Asmara’s sustained sovereignty rhetoric is not merely a response to a perceived threat, but rather part of a broader political narrative intended to legitimize an increasingly confrontational posture against Ethiopia. The latest intelligence allegations suggest that the regime’s preparations further extend beyond rhetorical and diplomatic confrontation to both indirect and potentially direct military action against the Ethiopian state. Sudan’s military regime is following an increasingly troubling trajectory of its own. Despite repeated Ethiopian efforts to prevent the deterioration of bilateral relations, facilitate an end to Sudan’s devastating internal conflict and encourage an inclusive civilian-led political transition, SAF under al-Burhan has increasingly adopted hostile rhetoric towards Addis Ababa. Ethiopia has consistently advocated a negotiated settlement to Sudan’s war, maintained humanitarian solidarity with the Sudanese population and continued electricity supplies to its neighbour. It has also refrained from officially taking sides in the conflict between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). Rather, Ethiopia’s Prime Minister was the first world leader to visit Port Sudan after SAF was driven out of Khartoum by the RSF, offering solidarity and support for the peace process in Sudan. Yet SAF rejected it, and has continued advancing allegations that Ethiopia is supporting the RSF, constructing an increasingly elaborate narrative around claims that Addis Ababa categorically rejects. Ethiopia has had legitimate security and strategic considerations that could inform its position on the Sudanese conflict, particularly given the implications of armed movements operating along its western borders and the regional consequences of Sudan’s fragmentation. Nevertheless, Addis Ababa has maintained its declared neutrality rather than formally aligning itself with either belligerent. The persistence of SAF’s accusations, despite Ethiopia’s stated diplomatic efforts and restraint, raises questions about whether the allegations are genuinely intended to address security concerns or are increasingly being used as instruments of political and diplomatic pressure against Ethiopia. That contradiction became particularly evident when Sudan submitted its letter to the United Nations Security Council on 30 October 2026, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter and claiming the right to self-defence against Ethiopia. In its communication, circulated as document S/2026/872, Khartoum accused Addis Ababa of facilitating drone attacks against Sudanese territory and supporting the RSF. Ethiopia rejected the allegations in its response of 6 November, document S/2026/892, describing them as unfounded and presenting its own account of SAF’s hostile activities, including alleged cross-border military violations, support for Ethiopian armed opposition movements and cooperation with forces seeking to undermine the Ethiopian government. Ethiopia also accused SAF of providing logistical assistance, weapons and equipment to TPLF-linked armed formations operating from Sudan. The invocation of self-defence is particularly consequential. Article 51 is not a diplomatic instrument to be invoked simply to elevate political accusations into claims of imminent military confrontation; its application rests on specific legal and factual conditions. Sudan’s decision to invoke it against Ethiopia, despite Addis Ababa’s declared neutrality and the absence of any established Ethiopian armed attack against Sudan, stands in sharp contrast to Ethiopia’s account of SAF’s own conduct and its substantiated coordination with hostile actors. These developments are unfolding alongside the growing political and diplomatic convergence between Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan. The October 4 quadrilateral summit in El Alamein, attended by Egypt’s Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrea’s Isaias Afwerki, Sudan’s al-Burhan and Somalia’a Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, was followed by the November 21 trilateral meeting of the Egyptian, Eritrean and Sudanese foreign ministers in Aswan. The convergence of strategic interests among these governments warrants close scrutiny, particularly against the backdrop of their increasingly difficult relations with Addis Ababa. Egypt’s longstanding strategic competition with Ethiopia over the Nile and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, Eritrea’s sustained hostility towards the Ethiopian state, and SAF’s increasingly confrontational posture create an alignment of interests with potentially serious consequences for regional stability. The reported Eritrean-Sudanese coordination over possible attacks against Ethiopian cities, coming days after the Aswan meeting, makes the timing particularly concerning. The broader pattern also raises legitimate questions about whether political coordination could increasingly translate into security cooperation and the use of proxy networks to exert pressure on Addis Ababa. What emerges is a troubling regional picture in which Ethiopia’s internal security challenges are increasingly intersecting with the strategic calculations of neighbouring governments. And the ongoing preparations to target Mekelle and Asosa represent a serious escalation with implications far beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Any attack on Ethiopian territory or civilian infrastructure would constitute an act of war and risk drawing the wider Horn of Africa into a far more dangerous confrontation. Ethiopia has repeatedly maintained that it seeks peaceful relations with its neighbours and a negotiated resolution to regional disputes. But restraint should not be mistaken for an absence of resolve. The consequences of turning regional rivalries into direct aggression against Ethiopia could prove far greater than anticipated By Horn Review Editorial Share this post Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Google + Email Author HORN REVIEW Leave a Reply Cancel reply Your email address will not be published. ethiopia.summary: Leaked intelligence suggests a troubling coordination between Eritrea and Sudan to conduct drone attacks on Ethiopian cities, specifically Mekelle and Assosa. This alleged collaboration indicates a significant escalation in hostilities, moving beyond proxy warfare to direct assaults on civilian targets. The Eritrean regime, led by Isaias Afwerki, has historically portrayed Ethiopia's maritime ambitions as a threat, while simultaneously supporting armed opposition groups against Ethiopia. Recent incursions by Eritrean forces into Ethiopian territory further complicate the already strained relations. Sudan's military leadership under General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has also adopted a hostile stance towards Ethiopia, despite Ethiopia's efforts to maintain neutrality and humanitarian support amid Sudan's internal conflict. The invocation of self-defense by Sudan against Ethiopia raises concerns about potential military confrontations. The convergence of interests among Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt poses a significant risk to regional stability, with the potential for direct aggression against Ethiopia threatening broader conflict in the Horn of Africa.

ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia and Djibouti are engaging in discussions aimed at enhancing port efficiency and improving trade corridors in anticipation of the upcoming rainy season. The talks focus on optimizing the logistics and transportation systems that connect the two nations, which are vital for Ethiopia's access to international markets through Djibouti's ports. Both countries recognize the importance of these improvements to facilitate smoother trade operations and mitigate potential disruptions caused by seasonal weather changes. The collaboration is expected to bolster economic ties and ensure that goods can be transported more effectively, benefiting both economies. As the rainy season approaches, the urgency of these discussions highlights the need for proactive measures to maintain trade flow and address any challenges that may arise. The outcomes of these talks could significantly impact regional trade dynamics and economic stability for both Ethiopia and Djibouti.

ethiopia.content: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 24, 2026 - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: All of Africa Today - November 24, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 24 November 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Amnesty Seeks War Crimes Probe Into Deadly Ethiopia Attacks Amnesty International is calling for an investigation into possible war crimes following artillery attacks by Ethiopian government forces and their Tigray Peace Forces allies that killed at least 14 civilians in Alamata, northern Tigray, between 26 and 28 September. The organisation said the shelling struck densely populated neighbourhoods, including residential homes and commercial areas, and injured numerous others. Amnesty also found that Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters had established military bases in residential areas and schools, putting civilians at risk. However, it stressed that this did not justify indiscriminate attacks and called for an independent international investigation and accountability for those responsible. The Ethiopian military and its allies had not responded to Amnesty's allegations at the time of publication, while the TPLF rejected the claims against its forces. Sudan Famine Driven by War, Not Natural Disaster – Report Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Nearly 19.5 million people in Sudan are facing crisis levels of hunger or worse, with the risk of famine remaining high in several parts of the country, according to the World Food Programme and a report by the Somoud Alliance. The ongoing war, displacement, restrictions on humanitarian aid, destruction of farmland and markets, and rising food prices have worsened food insecurity, with around five million people facing emergency levels of hunger and 135,000 in catastrophic conditions. An estimated 825,000 children under five are also expected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026. The alliance has called for an immediate ceasefire, safe humanitarian access and increased international funding to prevent further loss of life. It warned that funding shortages are leaving many households with only half their food rations, while attacks on aid workers and convoys continue to obstruct relief efforts. DR Congo Fighting Traps Ebola Responders in Hospital Heavy fighting near a hospital in the Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ituri province has forced Ebola responders and World Health Organization staff to shelter in a maternity ward for more than 24 hours. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said teams were working to evacuate trapped staff safely and called for protection for healthcare workers, patients, and medical facilities. The violence has disrupted efforts to contain the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak, with Ituri accounting for more than two-thirds of confirmed cases. The outbreak has recorded 11,762 confirmed cases and 5,775 deaths across eight provinces, according to figures released on 20 November. The WHO has also verified more than 87 attacks on healthcare facilities and workers in the DR Congo since the beginning of the year. Borno School Enrolment Nearly Doubles After Years of Boko Haram Violence Education is gradually recovering in Nigeria's northeastern Borno State after more than a decade of Boko Haram violence forced schools to close and displaced thousands of families. Government figures show enrolment in public and private schools increased to 1.4 million learners in 2025, up from about 766,000 during the 2017-2018 academic year. Authorities said that they have built 104 new schools and renovated nearly 3,000 classrooms. The number of out-of-school children has reportedly fallen from 2.2 million to fewer than 800,000. However, insecurity, poverty, teacher shortages and limited access to schools in rural communities continue to threaten efforts to restore education. Officials said that rebuilding confidence among parents and ensuring children receive adequate learning support remain key to sustaining the progress. Zimbabwean Preacher Uebert Angel Arrested on Sexual Assault Allegations Prominent Zimbabwean preacher Uebert Angel has been arrested in Harare on allegations of indecent assault and sodomy. The founder of Spirit Embassy was reportedly detained during a church service. The police are yet to provide details about the allegations or confirm when he will appear in court. Angel, who was appointed Zimbabwe's special presidential envoy and ambassador-at-large in 2021. He previously faced controversy following a 2023 Al Jazeera undercover investigation that alleged he offered to use his diplomatic status to facilitate money laundering through a gold-smuggling scheme. He has also previously faced allegations of sexual impropriety, which he denied. A member of his team confirmed that he remained in police custody. The timing of his court appearance was still unclear. Final Verdict Due in Senegal-Morocco AFCON Title Dispute The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) is set to deliver its ruling on Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip the country of its 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title and award it to Morocco. Senegal initially won the January final 1-0 after extra time, but the Confederation of African Football's appeals board overturned the result in March, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match after players walked off the pitch in protest over a controversial penalty decision. Morocco was subsequently awarded a 3-0 victory. Senegal's football federation challenged the decision, describing it as unfair, and is seeking to have the original result reinstated. The ruling could have wider implications for CAF's credibility and the application of tournament regulations. CAS's decision will be final, barring limited grounds for a further appeal before Switzerland's highest court, potentially bringing an end to the months-long dispute. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia, Norway Vow to Deepen Strategic Partnership On Climate Action and Sustainable Development - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia, Norway Vow to Deepen Strategic Partnership On Climate Action and Sustainable Development 23 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia and Norway have reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation on climate finance, forest conservation and multilateral development partnerships. Minister of Finance Fitsum Assefa held a bilateral meeting today with a Norwegian delegation led by Åsmund Grøver Aukrust, Minister of International Development of Norway, accompanied by Ambassador-Designate Yngvild Berggrav. The discussions reaffirmed the longstanding partnership between Ethiopia and Norway in sustainable land management, forest conservation and climate action. The two sides also discussed ways of opportunities to mobilize additional resources and strengthen international support for Ethiopia's climate and environmental priorities. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The ministers also discussed preparations for a major carbon-credit transaction and afforestation initiative, alongside Ethiopia's priorities ahead of COP32 in 2027. Minister of Finance Fitsum highlighted Ethiopia's climate priorities, including land restoration and the Green Legacy Initiative, as well as the Green Legacy and Degraded Landscape Restoration Special Fund, which aims to mobilize domestic and partner financing for climate action and landscape restoration. She also encouraged Norway to champion these priorities internationally and support efforts to mobilize long-term climate finance. State Minister Tiguist Fisseha briefed the Norwegian delegation on Ethiopia's Homegrown Economic Reform Agenda, including macroeconomic reforms and efforts to integrate climate risks into fiscal risk management. She expressed appreciation for the Norwegian Government's longstanding support to Ethiopia through bilateral cooperation and its contributions and engagement through multilateral development banks (MDBs). She also reiterated Ethiopia's appreciation for the support provided through the World Bank's International Development Association (IDA) in advancing the country's development priorities, supporting economic transformation and mobilizing resources for climate action and sustainable development. She underscored the importance of continued IDA support in the context of the upcoming IDA Mid-Term Review. The two sides agreed to further strengthen cooperation on climate change, forest conservation and sustainable development, building on shared priorities and pursuing opportunities of mutual benefit. somalia.content: Somalia Detects Only 42 Percent of Tuberculosis Cases Amid Deepening Crisis HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Somalia Detects Only 42 Percent of Tuberculosis Cases Amid Deepening Crisis by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Somalia Detects Only 42 Percent of Tuberculosis Cases Amid Deepening Crisis Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram Somalia ranks among the world’s 30 high-burden tuberculosis countries, recording an estimated incidence of 246 cases per 100,000 people and approximately 43,000 new cases in 2022. Mortality associated with the disease reaches approximately 63 individuals per 100,000 annually. Although treatment success for drug-sensitive tuberculosis reaches 87 percent, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is increasing, leading to Somalia’s classification as a high-burden country for drug-resistant strains. The national case detection rate is estimated at 42 percent by the World Health Organization, derived by comparing reported notifications against modeled incidence figures based on surveillance, prevalence surveys, and expert consensus. Because non-diagnosed cases are inferred through these models rather than directly counted, more than half of all infections remain undetected in communities. The National TB Strategic Plan 2024–2026 outlines planned efforts to improve direct burden measurement, including a national prevalence survey. Standard treatment for drug-sensitive tuberculosis spans six months, whereas regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis require up to 18 months. Managing drug-resistant cases is further constrained by infrastructure limitations, as specialized treatment is accessible at only 11 centers nationwide. This centralized distribution forces patients to travel extensive distances while managing regimens that carry severe side effects without sustained food support. Transmission dynamics remain closely tied to broader humanitarian distress across the country, where over 3.9 million internally displaced persons reside in overcrowded camps characterized by poor ventilation. Decades of recurrent drought, flooding, and conflict have devastated local livelihoods, leaving over 70 percent of the population living below the poverty line and amplifying conditions that facilitate airborne spread. Underlying nutritional deficits compound vulnerability to infection, with acute food insecurity affecting nearly half of all Somali households. The interaction between undernutrition and tuberculosis is bidirectional: compromised nutrition weakens immune defenses against infection, while active disease produces appetite loss and nutrient malabsorption. Patients frequently face severe side effects when taking antimicrobial medication on empty stomachs. Diagnostic access remains severely restricted for rural residents, nomadic pastoralists, and displaced populations, while pediatric tuberculosis cases are systematically underdiagnosed. Diagnostic delays are common because many individuals initially seek care from private practitioners who lack specific training in tuberculosis identification. Fragmented surveillance, manual recordkeeping, and an absence of digital reporting tools prevent timely outbreak tracking. The private healthcare sector comprises approximately 3,300 facilities and delivers an estimated 60 percent of health services across Somalia, but it accounts for only 15.4 percent of national tuberculosis case notifications. Formal engagement mechanisms between private entities and the National Tuberculosis Program remain limited. Supply chain bottlenecks further disrupt treatment continuity through recurring drug stockouts and maintenance demands that exceed local capacity. Economic barriers present severe obstacles to completing therapy, with 68 percent of tuberculosis-affected households experiencing catastrophic health expenditures. Defined by the World Health Organization as out-of-pocket medical payments exceeding 20 percent of total household income or consumption, these costs encompass transportation fares and lost household wages. Ongoing population displacement and physical insecurity continually disrupt adherence among nomadic and displaced groups. Somalia’s tuberculosis infrastructure is heavily dependent on international donor assistance, including 504 million dollars provided by the Global Fund since 2002, with 160 million dollars dedicated to tuberculosis control between 2022 and 2026. However, international funding reductions in 2025 resulted in the suspension of 125.5 million dollars in USAID aid, leading to the loss of more than 6,000 health worker jobs, affecting up to 2,000 facilities, and closing 37 health and nutrition facilities in and around Baidoa. In response to disrupted outreach, staff layoffs, and detection setbacks, public health priorities emphasize decentralizing case detection via mobile clinics and community workers in high-risk displacement settings. Additional priorities include integrating direct food assistance into clinical regimens, formalizing private sector partnerships to raise notification contributions to at least 20 percent by 2026, adopting shorter all-oral regimens for drug resistance, and securing multi-year contingency funding buffers. Epidemiological evaluation of tuberculosis in fragile settings requires distinguishing between directly observed notifications and inferred disease burden. The 42 percent case detection rate calculated for Somalia by the World Health Organization is established through a defined mathematical relationship: notified cases divided by estimated incidence multiplied by 100. Because routine surveillance captures only a portion of transmission, estimated incidence is derived from models synthesizing surveillance records, prevalence surveys, and expert consensus. The resulting unobserved cases do not represent directly counted individuals, but reflect the gap between modeled incidence and reported notifications. This gap indicates that over half of all infections remain unrecorded, forming an unobserved reservoir that sustains transmission. To transition from modeled estimates to empirical measurement, the National TB Strategic Plan 2024–2026 outlines priorities to improve burden tracking, including a national prevalence survey. Clinical observations in humanitarian displacement settings illustrate the biological interaction between nutritional deprivation and antimicrobial therapy. In the displacement camps of Galkayo, patients such as Faadumo take antimicrobial tablets with water after enduring extended periods without food. This circumstance reflects broader food insecurity affecting nearly half of all Somali households, where malnutrition weakens human immune defenses and increases susceptibility to infection. The biological relationship between tuberculosis and nutrition is bidirectional: compromised nutrition impairs host immunity, while active tuberculosis infection induces severe appetite loss and nutrient malabsorption, creating a self-reinforcing physiological cycle. Documenting this clinical barrier, Dr. Jarmilla Kliescikova of Médecins Sans Frontières noted that the human body cannot successfully combat an infection in the absence of metabolic fuel, concluding that food functions not as a secondary comfort, but as an indispensable component of clinical treatment. Completing chemotherapy regimens presents severe physical and economic obstacles for affected populations. Standard medical treatment for drug-sensitive tuberculosis requires a six-month antimicrobial course, whereas therapeutic regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis demand up to 18 months of continuous medication. When patients experience acute food deprivation, consuming heavy antimicrobial compounds on empty stomachs provokes severe physical side effects, frequently leading individuals to skip scheduled doses. These treatment disruptions occur alongside catastrophic economic burdens, with 68 percent of tuberculosis-affected households experiencing catastrophic health expenditures. Under the World Health Organization standard, catastrophic health expenditure is defined as out-of-pocket medical payments exceeding 20 percent of total household consumption or income. These financial losses encompass transportation fares to clinical facilities and forfeited household wages, with physical insecurity and population mobility further disrupting medication adherence among nomadic and internally displaced groups. Access to timely diagnostic services remains severely restricted across remote geographic areas and underserved populations. Diagnostic testing remains largely out of reach for nomadic pastoralists, rural communities, and internally displaced populations, while pediatric tuberculosis remains systematically underdiagnosed across clinical settings. Furthermore, widespread diagnostic delays occur because ill individuals frequently seek preliminary care from commercial healthcare providers who lack clinical training in tuberculosis diagnosis, inadvertently extending infectious periods. Although approximately 3,300 private facilities provide an estimated 60 percent of healthcare throughout Somalia, they generate only 15.4 percent of national tuberculosis notifications. Commercial facilities lack digital reporting platforms, finding manual paperwork burdensome, which leads to routine data loss and reporting delays that prevent health authorities from executing real-time outbreak responses. Although national targets aim to increase private notification contributions to at least 20 percent by 2026, progress is impeded by informal partnerships, weak regulatory structures, and fragmented data systems. Structural limitations in laboratory infrastructure and drug supply chains further complicate clinical disease management. Recurring pharmaceutical stockouts continually threaten treatment continuity, while laboratory equipment maintenance requirements frequently exceed local technical capacity. Managing drug-resistant tuberculosis is particularly constrained because second-line regimens require expensive pharmaceuticals associated with severe adverse side effects. These specialized therapies are accessible at only 11 authorized treatment centers across the entire country, forcing patients to travel vast distances from remote regions to obtain necessary care. Currently, the national health response lacks sustained nutritional assistance programs for the majority of tuberculosis patients, leaving a substantial supportive gap that accelerates the development of drug-resistant strains. Somalia’s disease control apparatus remains profoundly vulnerable to the volatility of international donor financing. Long-term assistance has depended heavily on external partners, with the Global Fund providing 504 million dollars since 2002, including 160 million dollars designated for tuberculosis programming between 2022 and 2026. However, international funding reductions in 2025 resulted in the suspension of 125.5 million dollars in USAID aid, producing acute operational shocks across the healthcare system. The funding suspension led to the closure of 37 health and nutrition facilities in and around Baidoa, disrupted services across up to 2,000 healthcare sites, and eliminated more than 6,000 healthcare worker positions. Following these budget cancellations, the National Tuberculosis Program documented disrupted case detection activities, curtailed community outreach, and extensive layoffs of essential clinical personnel. Addressing the national tuberculosis crisis requires implementing coordinated operational reforms across clinical, diagnostic, and logistical domains. Priority strategies outlined in national frameworks emphasize decentralizing diagnostic testing by deploying community health workers and mobile clinics to reach nomadic and displaced groups in remote environments, accompanied by active case-finding campaigns in high-risk displacement camps and food-insecure districts. Clinical protocols must integrate sustained nutritional assistance, providing food baskets or direct cash transfers to every patient throughout the full duration of treatment. Furthermore, managing drug-resistant tuberculosis requires transitioning toward shorter, all-oral regimens and establishing decentralized treatment initiation at the district level. Sustaining these clinical measures requires predictable multi-year financing commitments from international donors alongside dedicated contingency buffers for essential medical commodities. As clinical correspondence notes, addressing months-long diagnostic delays, preventing pediatric deaths arising from vaccine shortages, and ensuring patients do not take medication on empty stomachs represent collective public health responsibilities rather than technical impossibilities. somalia.title: Somalia Coastal Spring Shows Low Mineralization and Favorable Baseline Drinking Water Quality - Bioengineer.org
somalia.content: Somalia Coastal Spring Shows Low Mineralization and Favorable Baseline HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 25, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Technology Somalia Coastal Spring Shows Low Mineralization and Favorable Baseline Drinking Water Quality by November 24, 2026 in Technology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Somalia Coastal Spring Shows Low Mineralization and Favorable Baseline Drinking Water Quality Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on Linkedin Share on Reddit Share on Telegram A hydrogeochemical baseline assessment conducted at the Ildabey Spring in the coastal district of Eyl, northeastern Somalia, revealed that the emerging freshwater source exhibited low overall dissolved solids, circumneutral to slightly alkaline conditions, and chemical characteristics consistent with accepted drinking-water standards during the January 2026 dry season. Across the surveyed system in Puntland State, water samples collected along a short surface-flow channel demonstrated electrical conductivity values averaging 336 microsiemens per centimeter and total dissolved solids averaging 213 milligrams per liter, remaining well below international drinking-water thresholds. The investigation, carried out along an arid coastal environment where natural springs serve as vital municipal resources, established an integrated benchmark combining major-ion measurements, thermodynamic mineral saturation modeling, multivariate statistics, and a ten-parameter weighted arithmetic Water Quality Index to clarify baseline conditions in an understudied region of the Horn of Africa. Natural groundwater and emergence springs constitute fundamental components of water security across arid and semi-arid landscapes, especially in regions confronting recurrent drought, high potential evaporation rates, and an absence of dependable perennial river systems. In northeastern Somalia, sedimentary geological successions composed predominantly of Mesozoic to Cenozoic carbonate and siliciclastic strata, together with fractured and unconsolidated coastal formations, govern regional groundwater occurrence and flow. The Ildabey Spring represents a perennial freshwater discharge feature in Eyl District within the Nugal Region, emerging directly from subsurface fractured sedimentary units before traveling through an open rocky bed into a natural pooling basin. Because coastal aquifers in data-scarce environments face long-term vulnerabilities from climate variability, domestic abstraction pressures, and potential seawater intrusion, developing an empirical, localized baseline represents an indispensable prerequisite for future water-resource monitoring and resource protection strategies. To evaluate the spatial distribution of dissolved constituents along the spring channel, the research team established twelve fixed sampling stations organized into three distinct geographic zones representing the surface-flow sequence. Zone A captured the spring emergence point at approximately 7.9833 degrees North and 49.8167 degrees East, where subsurface water first breaches the ground; Zone B represented an intermediate, rocky-bottomed transport segment downstream of the outlet; and Zone C encompassed the downstream natural collection basin characterized by reduced flow velocity and sediment accumulation. Field sampling was conducted on January 8, January 16, and January 24, 2026, generating thirty-six total field observations from repeat visits across the twelve fixed stations. Pre-cleaned high-density polyethylene containers and zero-point-forty-five-micrometer cellulose membrane filtration were used for collection, while temperature, pH, electrical conductivity, dissolved oxygen, and total dissolved solids were recorded directly in situ with calibrated multiparameter field instruments. Subsequent laboratory determinations followed rigorous analytical protocols, utilizing flame photometry for sodium and potassium, fast sequential atomic absorption spectrometry for calcium and magnesium, ion chromatography for chloride, sulfate, nitrate, and fluoride, and standardized acid titration for total alkalinity. Rigorous quality assurance protocols maintained instrument calibration curves with coefficients of determination of zero-point-nine-nine-nine or greater and drift within five percent, alongside procedural blanks and analytical replicates. In the resulting dataset, charge-balance calculations achieved arithmetic closure within narrow decimal tolerances, functioning as a measure of numerical computational consistency rather than standalone verification of external analytical accuracy. For zone-level statistical inferences, the researchers avoided inflating sample sizes by averaging the three temporal visits into twelve independent location-level means, yielding four spatial replicates per zone to evaluate channel gradients without overstating spatial independence. Across the entire thirty-six-visit dataset, physicochemical parameters exhibited remarkable consistency and narrow descriptive distributions. The overall mean water temperature was 25.2 degrees Celsius, while pH averaged 7.30, varying from 7.18 in the emergence zone to 7.42 in the downstream pool. Turbidity remained low throughout, averaging 1.08 nephelometric turbidity units with an overall range of 0.58 to 1.66 NTU. Mean total hardness was 137 milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate, while alkalinity averaged 159 milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate. Dissolved oxygen remained elevated at an average of 6.83 milligrams per liter, although it decreased from 7.14 milligrams per liter at the spring outlet to 6.48 milligrams per liter in the downstream collection pool. Specific nutrient and halogen concentrations were similarly moderate, yielding overall mean values of 4.73 milligrams per liter for nitrate, 18.4 milligrams per liter for sulfate, 23.4 milligrams per liter for chloride, and 0.52 milligrams per liter for fluoride, with all parameters remaining within the study’s adopted World Health Organization reference guidelines. Despite the generally low absolute mineralization, one-way analysis of variance across the location means revealed statistically significant downstream increases for almost every measured dissolved constituent between Zone A and Zone C. Electrical conductivity climbed steadily from 287 microsiemens per centimeter at the spring emergence to 334 in the rocky channel and 386 in the collection pool, mirrored by total dissolved solids increasing from 181 to 213 and 244 milligrams per liter. Tukey post-hoc tests confirmed significant differences among all three zones for electrical conductivity, dissolved solids, hardness, alkalinity, nitrate, sulfate, chloride, and fluoride, while temperature differed significantly between the emergence point and the terminal pool. Exploratory spatial mapping using inverse distance weighting illustrated these gradual longitudinal increments, though the authors emphasized that the twelve-point layout across a linear channel cannot exclude localized, unmeasured variations occurring between sampling points. Converting major dissolved constituents into milliequivalents per liter established that calcium was the dominant dissolved cation, followed by sodium and magnesium, while bicarbonate constituted the overwhelming majority of dissolved anions. Calcium contributed approximately forty-six-point-six to forty-seven-point-zero percent of the total cation equivalent budget, magnesium represented sixteen-point-three to sixteen-point-five percent, and combined alkali cations accounted for the remaining thirty-six to thirty-seven percent. Potassium concentrations were minor and constant at zero-point-zero-three-two milliequivalents per liter across all zones. On Gibbs classification diagrams, the spring water samples plotted entirely within the rock-dominance field, showing low ratios of sodium to calcium and chloride to bicarbonate, which strongly suggests that chemical acquisition was driven primarily by water-rock interaction rather than atmospheric precipitation inputs or extensive evaporative concentration. Geochemical interpretations and speciation modeling using PHREEQC provided additional insight into the thermodynamic equilibria governing the spring water. Calculated saturation indices for calcite and dolomite hovered near zero, indicating states approaching thermodynamic equilibrium with carbonate rock matrices, whereas gypsum, halite, and fluorite exhibited strongly negative saturation indices reflecting undersaturation. The researchers observed that while undersaturation confirms that mineral dissolution remains thermodynamically feasible if those minerals exist in the flow path, it does not prove active dissolution rates or mineral abundance. Furthermore, Schoeller chloro-alkaline indices yielded negative values across all samples, with index one ranging from negative one-point-seventy-seven to negative one-point-sixteen and index two ranging from negative zero-point-twenty-eight to negative zero-point-twenty-three. Although such negative indices are compatible with base-exchange reactions where dissolved calcium and magnesium exchange for sodium in surrounding materials, they may also reflect mixed lithological inputs and subsurface circulation pathways. Exploratory multivariate statistical routines including Pearson correlation, Principal Component Analysis, and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis summarized the covariance architecture of the thirty-six field observations. Strong positive correlations emerged among electrical conductivity, dissolved solids, hardness, alkalinity, sulfate, and chloride, while dissolved oxygen exhibited negative associations with dissolved mineralization. Principal Component Analysis extracted three components explaining eighty-four-point-thirty-seven percent of the cumulative dataset variance, with the first component accounting for fifty-one-point-eighty-four percent and dominated by high positive loadings for mineralization-related variables, while the second component captured dissolved oxygen, pH, and fluoride. Hierarchical clustering grouped variables into three coherent statistical clusters, separating primary mineralization constituents from equilibrium buffering parameters and minor environmental inputs; however, the authors noted that these groupings reflect mathematical associations among correlated indicators rather than independently validated, distinct physical contamination sources. Application of the ten-parameter weighted arithmetic Water Quality Index generated mean ratings of 23.11 in Zone A, 30.41 in Zone B, and 36.22 in Zone C, classifying the emergence point as excellent and downstream waters as good for drinking purposes. Parameter sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the index score was highly sensitive to the inclusion of fluoride due to its heavy mathematical weight, whereas removing alkalinity caused negligible numerical variation. Crucially, the authors underscored that physicochemical indices alone cannot verify microbiological safety or the absence of toxic trace elements such as lead, arsenic, or cadmium. Because the study was deliberately confined to a short dry-season transect within a single spring channel, the authors concluded that these favorable baseline numbers must serve as a launchpad for future multi-season monitoring programs incorporating bacterial assays, isotopic tracers, and hydrological discharge measurements before wider public-health guarantees or regional aquifer generalizations can be established. somalia.summary: A hydrogeochemical assessment of the Ildabey Spring in Eyl, northeastern Somalia, has revealed promising results regarding its water quality. Conducted during the dry season in January 2026, the study found that the spring exhibited low mineralization levels, with total dissolved solids averaging 213 mg/L and electrical conductivity at 336 microsiemens/cm, both well within international drinking-water standards. The research involved extensive sampling across three geographic zones, highlighting the spring's significance as a freshwater resource in an arid region. The analysis utilized various scientific methods, including multivariate statistics and a ten-parameter Water Quality Index, which rated the water quality as excellent to good for drinking. Despite these favorable findings, the authors emphasized the need for ongoing monitoring to assess microbiological safety and potential contamination from trace elements. This study serves as a crucial baseline for future water resource management in a region vulnerable to climate variability and water scarcity. (158 words)

somalia.content: Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia, Uganda agree to strengthen security cooperation against al-Shabab Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni have called for intensified military operations against al-Shabab and alternative funding arrangements to sustain Ugandan troops deployed in Somalia, as uncertainty grows over the future of African Union peacekeeping operations. In a joint communiqué issued Monday, Nov. 23, following talks in Entebbe, Uganda, the two leaders emphasized the need for adequate, predictable and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) and closer military cooperation to combat the al-Qaeda-linked militant group. advertisements The discussions came during Hassan Sheikh's one-day official visit to Uganda at Museveni's invitation, as Kampala begins a phased withdrawal of troops deployed under bilateral security arrangements with Somalia. The two presidents called on AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces to increase offensive operations against al-Shabab while exploring alternative financing mechanisms for forces operating under bilateral agreements. They also urged closer coordination among countries contributing troops to the African Union mission to strengthen counterterrorism operations and preserve security gains achieved over nearly two decades. The leaders praised the contributions of the Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF), Somali troops and other African Union peacekeepers, paying tribute to soldiers killed or wounded during operations against al-Shabab. They reaffirmed their commitment to consolidating security gains achieved under AUSSOM and its predecessor missions, the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS) and the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM). The presidents also referred to decisions reached during an extraordinary summit of AUSSOM troop-contributing countries held in Kampala on July 31, where leaders called for a coordinated security transition and sustained international financial assistance. Uganda, one of the largest contributors to African Union military operations in Somalia since 2007, began withdrawing troops deployed under bilateral arrangements earlier this month. The Ugandan military has also announced plans for a gradual withdrawal of its AUSSOM contingent by the end of 2027, raising concerns about potential security gaps in areas previously protected by its forces. However, Monday's communiqué did not announce any changes to Uganda's withdrawal timetable or confirm whether additional funding had been secured. Beyond military cooperation, Hassan Sheikh and Museveni emphasized the importance of political reconciliation and cooperation between Somalia's federal government, federal member states and other stakeholders. The leaders called for stronger relations through dialogue, good governance and peacebuilding to support security, stability and economic development. Their appeal comes as Somalia faces political disagreements over constitutional amendments, the mandates of federal institutions and the timetable for national elections. Opposition groups and the administrations of Puntland and Jubaland have rejected constitutional changes extending presidential and parliamentary terms, calling for a negotiated political settlement. The federal government maintains that the amendments provide a legal basis for elections scheduled in 2027. The joint communiqué did not announce any mediation initiative or specific agreement to resolve the political dispute. The two presidents also reviewed progress in bilateral economic cooperation, welcoming agreements and decisions reached during the Somalia-Uganda Joint Business Forum and Exhibition held in Mogadishu from Oct. 20 to 22. They welcomed the signing of a bilateral labor agreement and the agreed terms for a Bilateral Air Services Agreement aimed at expanding economic cooperation and transportation links. The leaders also revisited a proposal discussed during Hassan Sheikh's previous visit to Uganda on Oct. 26 to establish a warehouse in Mogadishu for Ugandan commercial goods. They agreed to continue considering the development of a port facility to facilitate trade and investment between the two countries. The proposals are intended to improve the movement of goods and expand commercial opportunities as Somalia and Uganda strengthen their economic partnership. Both leaders reaffirmed their commitment to regional integration through the East African Community, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa and the African Union. They also called on international partners to continue supporting Somalia's security institutions, humanitarian response and efforts to address climate change. The presidents welcomed logistical and operational assistance provided by the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS), which supports African Union peacekeeping operations and Somali security forces. At the conclusion of the visit, Hassan Sheikh invited Museveni to visit Somalia. The Ugandan president accepted the invitation, with the dates to be arranged through diplomatic channels. The joint communiqué was signed in Entebbe by Somalia's Foreign Minister Abdisalam Abdi Ali and Ugandan Foreign Minister Adonia Ayebare. They emphasized the need for intensified military operations and sustainable funding for the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), especially as Uganda begins a phased withdrawal of its troops. The leaders called for increased offensive actions by AUSSOM and the Somali National Armed Forces while exploring alternative financing for military operations. They also highlighted the importance of political reconciliation within Somalia amid ongoing disputes over constitutional amendments and election timelines. somalia.content: Saadaq Joon replaces Ahmed Moallim Fiqi as Somalia's defence minister - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Saadaq Joon replaces Ahmed Moallim Fiqi as Somalia's defence minister Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Monday November 23, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somali Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre appointed lawmaker Saadaq Omar Mohamed Hassan, widely known as Saadaq Joon, as the country's new defence minister on Monday, replacing Ahmed Moallim Fiqi in a limited Cabinet reshuffle that also affected two deputy ministers. In a decree issued Nov. 23, the Prime Minister's Office announced that Saadaq Joon would take over the Defence Ministry following Fiqi's departure from the position. advertisements The government did not specify why Fiqi left the ministry or announce whether he would be assigned another Cabinet position. Saadaq Joon, a member of Somalia's House of the People, previously served as commander of the Banadir Regional Police Force and has held several senior security positions. His appointment comes a day after Galmudug President Liibaan Ahmed Hassan announced a new regional Cabinet, following political changes in the central Somali state. According to political sources, Saadaq Joon's appointment is linked to a power-sharing arrangement between the federal government and former Galmudug President Ahmed Abdi Kaariye Qoorqoor following the election of Liibaan Ahmed Hassan. The reported arrangement is understood to involve the redistribution of senior government positions following the Galmudug leadership transition. However, the Prime Minister's Office did not publicly confirm that the defence appointment was part of a political agreement with Qoorqoor. The reshuffle also involved changes to two deputy ministerial positions. Ali Ifiye Ali was appointed deputy minister of ports and maritime transport, while Maryan Ali Abukar was named deputy minister of fisheries and the blue economy. The prime minister instructed the newly appointed officials to assume their responsibilities immediately and urged them to carry out their duties with integrity, dedication and accountability. Saadaq Joon takes over the Defence Ministry as Somalia continues military operations against al-Shabab and prepares to assume greater security responsibilities from African Union peacekeeping forces. The appointment also comes as the federal government and international partners discuss the future of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), whose current United Nations authorization expires Dec. 31. Fiqi had served as defence minister since April 2025, overseeing military operations against al-Shabab and cooperation with international security partners. somalia.content: Somalia's cabinet approves changes to election laws - TRT Afrika | English | English POLITICS AFRICA TÜRKİYE OPINION FEATURES SPORTS AFRICA 2 min read Somalia's cabinet approves changes to election laws The amendments are intended to bring the electoral laws in line with Somalia’s recent constitutional reform, according to the Prime Minister’s office. Share Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre chaired the cabinet meeting. / Other By Nuri Aden Somalia’s Council of Ministers on Tuesday approved changes to the country's electoral laws that determine how voters elect political representatives and how parties qualify for national recognition. The amendments were approved during an extraordinary cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Hamza Abdi Barre. RECOMMENDED Ethiopia offers to host talks on ending Sudan war, proposes unity government Libya's Government of National Unity denies prior deal with Ukraine over Benghazi attacks Paramilitary RSF spy chief defects to Sudanese army Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions RECOMMENDED Ethiopia offers to host talks on ending Sudan war, proposes unity government Libya's Government of National Unity denies prior deal with Ukraine over Benghazi attacks Paramilitary RSF spy chief defects to Sudanese army Senegal reinstated as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions In total, 23 provisions of the National Electoral Law and eight provisions of the Political Associations and Parties Law were affected. The amendments are intended to bring the two laws in line with Somalia’s recent constitutional reform, according to a statement from the Prime Minister’s office. Under the revised electoral framework, Somali citizens will directly elect members of local councils, federal member state legislatures and both houses of the Federal Parliament. However, government leaders including the president would be elected by their respective representative bodies rather than through a direct popular vote. The cabinet also approved provisions allowing the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission to establish procedures aimed at simplifying voter registration and voting, in accordance with constitutional requirements. Changes to political party system The proposed amendments to the Political Associations and Parties Law introduce a threshold requiring political organisations to secure at least 10 percent of votes in federal-level elections to qualify for recognition as national political parties. The cabinet also endorsed a closed-list electoral system, under which political parties would submit predetermined lists of parliamentary candidates. Under this arrangement, voters would cast ballots for political party lists rather than individual candidates, with seats allocated according to the applicable electoral rules. The changes come amid continuing political disagreements over Somalia’s electoral framework, with opposition groups and some federal member states calling for broader consultations on constitutional and electoral reforms. somalia.content: Nearly 400 health facilities shut down in Somalia following U.S. aid cuts, minister says - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Nearly 400 health facilities shut down in Somalia following U.S. aid cuts, minister says Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Tuesday November 24, 2026 Patients sit at the entrance of Banadir Hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia, on Tuesday, Nov. 11, 2025. (AP Photo/Farah Abdi Warsameh) License this photo Mogadishu (HOL) — Nearly 400 health facilities and several mobile medical units across Somalia have closed following the withdrawal of funding from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), Somalia's health minister said Monday. Speaking to reporters in Mogadishu on Nov. 23, Health and Social Care Minister Ali Haji Adan said the closures resulted from Somalia's heavy dependence on international donors to finance essential healthcare services. advertisements The minister said many of the affected facilities had relied on humanitarian assistance to provide medical care, but were unable to continue operating after U.S. funding was discontinued. He warned that Somalia's healthcare system remains vulnerable to changes in international assistance because a significant portion of community-level health services is financed by foreign donors. “The loss of funding has particularly affected health facilities operating through humanitarian programs and mobile medical teams that provide services to communities with limited access to permanent healthcare facilities,” he added. However, he did not identify the regions or districts where the facilities had closed or provide figures showing how many people had lost access to healthcare. Adan said nearly 600 other health facilities supported through longer-term health development programs remain operational across the country. He expressed hope that those facilities would continue delivering essential services despite the financial challenges affecting Somalia's health sector. The minister's remarks come as international humanitarian organizations warn that reductions in foreign assistance are placing increasing pressure on Somalia's already fragile healthcare system. Somalia depends heavily on donor-supported health programs to provide services such as maternal and child healthcare, vaccinations, disease prevention and treatment, particularly in rural areas and communities displaced by conflict and climate-related disasters. Funding shortages have raised concerns about the continuity of these services as humanitarian organizations face growing financial constraints. The closures also come as Somalia continues to face multiple humanitarian challenges, including recurring droughts, food insecurity, population displacement and outbreaks of preventable diseases. The health minister did not announce an emergency funding plan to reopen the affected facilities or provide a timetable for restoring services.
